To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
children younger than 11 years of old cannot learn the new spatial pattern of walking on split belts, and the spatial pattern they do acquire is similar to that of cerebellar patients.
children younger than 11 years old show deficits in the learning of new spatial coordination between the legs, whereas children older than 11 years and adults show normal learning.
the ability to learn and store spatial and temporal patterns of locomotion is not fully mature by late childhood, and that this is likely due to the developmental state of cerebellum.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how humans acquire and refine motor skills.
the development of motor learning and the maturation of cerebellar function.
how the brain adapts to new situations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the cerebellum is involved in learning of locomotor patterns in children, as well as in cerebellar patients.
the cerebellum is not the only brain structure involved in the acquisition and retention of locomotor adaptation.
the maturation of the cerebellar circuitry underlying motor adaptation is a slow process, with the cerebellar cortex being one of the last structures to mature.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ability to learn and store novel motor patterns matures over the course of childhood and adolescence.

the cerebellum plays a role in the development of locomotor adaptation, but it is not fully mature until the end of childhood, and that the maturation process is different for spatial versus temporal parameters.
the cerebellar contribution to the development of motor control is a long and gradual one.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children younger than 12 years old may be less able to learn a new motor skill than adults.
children are not just little adults and should not be treated as such when it comes to motor learning and adaptation.
the ability to learn new walking patterns is not fully mature until late childhood.
